meta.title: Canadian Immigration / Asylum / Enforcement Policy Events
meta.description: Curated, fully-sourced dated policy, legal and operational events that weakened or strengthened Canada's immigration screening, asylum, enforcement, removal and bail-courts systems. Designed to be overlaid against crime trends (trafficking, kidnapping, sexual assault, child exploitation).
meta.source_note: Immigration-instrument events harvested and verified from the repo's policy-timeline.html (IRCC / ESDC / CBSA news, Canada Gazette: P.C. 2016-981, P.C. 2024-161, IRPA s.87.3/s.94). Bail/courts and trafficking-law events verified against Parliament of Canada, the Supreme Court (CanLII) and Justice Canada. parliamentary_vote=True only for Acts of Parliament.

events.title: Protecting Canada's Immigration System Act (Bill C-31) — Designated Countries of Origin
events.summary: Created the Designated Countries of Origin (DCO) regime: claimants from 'safe' countries received faster processing and limited appeal rights, as a deterrent against low-merit claims. Royal assent 28 Jun 2012; in force 15 Dec 2012.
events.citation: Protecting Canada's Immigration System Act, S.C. 2012, c. 17 (Bill C-31, 41-1)

events.title: Bill C-452 (trafficking) — consecutive-sentencing provision never brought into force
events.summary: Private member's bill on exploitation and trafficking received royal assent in June 2015, but its mandatory consecutive-sentencing provision was left to come into force by order; that order was never made over s.12 Charter (cruel-and-unusual-punishment) concerns, so the toughest sentencing measure never took effect.
events.citation: An Act to amend the Criminal Code (exploitation and trafficking in persons), S.C. 2015, c. 16 (Bill C-452, 41-2)

events.title: R v Jordan — presumptive trial-delay ceilings (18/30 months)
events.summary: The Supreme Court set presumptive ceilings of 18 months (provincial court) and 30 months (superior court) from charge to end of trial; exceeding them is presumptively unreasonable under Charter s.11(b) and leads to a stay. The ruling increased pressure to drop or stay charges in a congested court system.
events.citation: R. v. Jordan, 2016 SCC 27, [2016] 1 SCR 631

events.title: Mexico visitor-visa requirement lifted
events.summary: Dropped the temporary-resident visa for Mexican citizens, leaving only the lighter eTA, via a regulation amending the IRPR (no parliamentary vote). Mexican asylum claims subsequently rose from ~260 (2016) to ~24,000 (2023), about 17% of all claims.
events.citation: P.C. 2016-981, regulations amending IRPR (SOR); Canada Gazette

events.title: Bill C-38 — trafficking presumption in force; consecutive sentencing dropped
events.summary: Brought into force most of former Bill C-452 — an exploitation presumption easing the prosecutor's burden and reverse-onus proceeds-of-crime forfeiture — but deliberately omitted the mandatory consecutive-sentencing provision because of s.12 Charter risk. Net: a partial strengthening of prosecution with the toughest penalty tool removed.
events.citation: An Act to amend An Act to amend the Criminal Code (exploitation and trafficking in persons), S.C. 2017, c. 13 (Bill C-38, 42-1)

events.title: Designated Countries of Origin regime emptied
events.summary: The government removed all countries from the DCO list, administratively ending the C-31 fast-track-deterrent for claims from low-acceptance countries; no legislation was needed to neutralise the statute's effect.
events.citation: IRCC news release, removal of all countries from the DCO list (May 2019)

events.title: Inland ineligibility for prior foreign claimants (Bill C-97, Div. 16)
events.summary: Made a claimant ineligible for an IRB hearing if they had already claimed asylum in an information-sharing country (US, UK, Australia, NZ). A narrow tightening, enacted inside the budget implementation act rather than debated as immigration law. Royal assent 21 Jun 2019.
events.citation: Budget Implementation Act, 2019, No. 1, S.C. 2019, c. 29 (Bill C-97, 42-1), Division 16

events.title: Bill C-75 — bail 'principle of restraint' codified
events.summary: Comprehensively revised interim-release (bail) provisions: codified a principle of restraint requiring release at the earliest opportunity on the least onerous conditions, with attention to vulnerable and Indigenous accused. Royal assent 21 Jun 2019; bail provisions in force 18 Dec 2019. Critics link it to higher release rates for repeat offenders.
events.citation: An Act to amend the Criminal Code, the Youth Criminal Justice Act and other Acts, S.C. 2019, c. 25 (Bill C-75, 42-1)

events.title: Auditor General report: CBSA lost track of removal-order subjects
events.summary: The Office of the Auditor General found CBSA did not know the whereabouts of ~34,700 people under enforceable removal orders (about two-thirds of sampled cases); failed asylum claimants were the largest group ordered to leave, most not removed within the one-year target. Documents the chronic enforcement gap at the system's exit.
events.citation: Office of the Auditor General of Canada, Spring 2020 Reports — Report 1, Immigration Removals (tabled 8 Jul 2020)

events.title: Temporary Foreign Worker 'Workforce Solutions Road Map'
events.summary: Loosened the TFW Program: LMIA validity extended 9->18 months; low-wage hiring cap raised from 10% to 20% (30% in seven sectors incl. food service); ended automatic refusal of low-wage LMIAs in high-unemployment regions. Rapidly enlarged the in-country temporary-worker pool from which inland claims are later made.
events.citation: ESDC, Workforce Solutions Road Map / TFW Program changes (4 Apr 2022)

events.title: Express Entry category-based selection authority (Bill C-19)
events.summary: IRPA amendments (in a budget bill) authorised the Minister to invite Express Entry candidates by category to meet economic goals, shifting selection toward ministerial discretion. First category-based draws ran 28 Jun 2023. A selection-design change rather than a direct asylum/enforcement lever.
events.citation: Budget Implementation Act, 2022, No. 1, S.C. 2022, c. 10 (Bill C-19, 44-1), IRPA amendments

events.title: Immigration Levels Plan: 500,000 permanent residents by 2025
events.summary: Tabled PR targets of 465k / 485k / 500k for 2023-25 — a growth-maximising posture that set the political ceiling to maximum. A permanent-resident plan and backdrop to the temporary surge, not a direct asylum or enforcement lever.
events.citation: Immigration Levels Plan 2023-2025, tabled under IRPA s.94 (1 Nov 2022)

events.title: International students left uncapped
events.summary: Through 2023 study-permit intake ran without a national ceiling and with weak oversight of bad-actor institutions, making the study-permit population the largest single feeder into the temporary pool — many later able to claim asylum when status lapsed.
events.citation: IRCC study-permit data, 2023 (pre-cap); see Jan 2024 cap announcement context

events.title: Safe Third Country Agreement extended to the whole land border
events.summary: The Additional Protocol let each country turn back irregular crossers who claim within 14 days, applying the STCA across the entire land border; Roxham Road closed the same day after ~100,000 crossings. It did not reduce claims but redirected them inland and to airports (inland share rose from 31% in 2022 toward 71% in 2025).
events.citation: Additional Protocol to the Canada-U.S. Safe Third Country Agreement (entered into force 25 Mar 2023)

events.title: Bill C-48 — bail reform (reverse onus for repeat violent offenders)
events.summary: Expanded reverse-onus bail provisions targeting serious repeat violent offending with weapons (firearms, knives, bear spray) and repeat intimate-partner violence, shifting the burden onto the accused to justify release. Royal assent 5 Dec 2023; in force 4 Jan 2024.
events.citation: An Act to amend the Criminal Code (bail reform), S.C. 2023, c. 30 (Bill C-48, 44-1)

events.title: Two-year cap on study-permit applications
events.summary: Capped applications accepted into processing (~606,250 for the year, ~360,000 approvals — a 35% cut from 2023) and required a provincial attestation letter, by ministerial instruction in the Canada Gazette. The first real brake, but it throttled new entries while those already admitted remained and increasingly claimed inland.
events.citation: Ministerial Instructions under IRPA s.87.3 (study-permit intake cap, 22 Jan 2024)

events.title: Mexico visa requirement partially reimposed
events.summary: Restored a visa requirement for many Mexican travellers (eTA kept only for existing work/study-permit holders), citing 'exponential growth' in claims — explicitly undoing the 2016 decision, eight years and tens of thousands of claims later.
events.citation: P.C. 2024-161, regulations amending IRPR (SOR); Canada Gazette

events.title: TFW low-wage stream tightened (reversing 2022 loosening)
events.summary: Reversed key 2022 loosenings: refused low-wage LMIA processing in metro areas with unemployment at or above 6%, cut the low-wage cap back toward 10% of a workforce, and shortened low-wage job-offer/employment durations — shrinking a major feeder into the in-country temporary pool.
events.citation: ESDC, changes to the Temporary Foreign Worker Program low-wage stream (effective 26 Sep 2024)

events.title: Asylum eligibility bars applied to claims on/after 3 Jun 2025
events.summary: New eligibility bars later codified in Bill C-12 apply to claims made on or after 3 Jun 2025: a one-year bar (claims more than a year after first entry since 24 Jun 2020 are not referred to the IRB) and a codified 14-day bar for between-ports land-border crossers. The claim-date trigger predates royal assent.
events.citation: Bill C-12 (45-1) transitional application date; IRCC announcement

events.title: Strengthening Canada's Immigration System and Borders Act (Bill C-12)
events.summary: Codified two new asylum eligibility bars (a one-year bar and a 14-day land-border bar), added real-time data-sharing across IRCC/CBSA/ESDC/provincial police and digital removal orders. Royal assent 26 Mar 2026; most provisions in force 1 Jan 2027. The first major legislative response — ~10 years after the executive decisions that built the channel, aimed mainly at new claims, not the existing backlog.
events.citation: Strengthening Canada's Immigration System and Borders Act (Bill C-12, 45-1), royal assent 26 Mar 2026
